title: Write for a variety of different purposes

lessons.title: Why we write and who we write for
lessons.html:
Writing at work and at home

We write for many reasons. On a farm or in a plant you may need to:

  • fill in a form, such as a leave form or a stock sheet;
  • write a short note or message for a co-worker;
  • write down a temperature, a count or a weight on a record sheet;
  • write an incident report after an accident;
  • write a letter, for example to apply for a job or a training course.

Each kind of writing has a purpose (why you write) and a reader (who will read it). Before you write, ask yourself two questions:

  1. Why am I writing? To tell, to ask, to record or to explain?
  2. Who will read it? A friend, a supervisor, the manager, a clinic, a government office?

Formal and informal writing

InformalFormal
A note to a friend or family memberA letter to the farm manager
"Hi Sipho, see you at the bus.""Dear Mr Botha, I would like to apply for..."
Short words and SMS language may be fineFull sentences, polite words, no SMS language

Write clearly

  • Use short sentences.
  • Put one idea in each sentence.
  • Start each sentence with a capital letter and end it with a full stop.
  • Write neatly so others can read it. Use a pen on records, not a pencil.
  • Write numbers, dates and names carefully – a wrong number on a feed sheet or a temperature record can cause big problems.

Good writing saves time. When your note or report is clear, the reader does not have to come and ask you what you meant.

lessons.title: Notes, messages and forms
lessons.html:
Short everyday writing

Writing a message

A good message answers: who, what, when and where.

To: Lindiwe
From: Peter
Date: Tuesday 14 May, 10:30
The vet phoned. She will come at 2 o'clock today to see the sick heifer in camp 6. Please make sure the crush is open.

Notice that the message has the name of the reader and writer, the date and time, and the important details.

Filling in forms

Forms ask for information in a fixed way. Follow these steps:

  1. Read the whole form first.
  2. Look for words like PRINT (write in capital letters), sign and tick.
  3. Write in the right boxes. Do not leave out parts that you need to fill in.
  4. Write N/A (not applicable) if a question does not apply to you.
  5. Check that names, ID number and dates are correct.
  6. Sign and date the form.
  7. Ask for help if you do not understand a question. Never sign something you do not understand.

Record sheets

At work you may write daily records: the number of eggs collected, the dip tank level, cold room temperatures, or hours worked. Write the date and time, the number, and your name or initials. If you make a mistake, draw one line through it, write the correct value next to it and initial it. Never use correction fluid or tear out pages on records.

Lists

Lists help you remember. A shopping list for the farm store or a list of jobs for the day is written one item per line. Put the most important item first.

lessons.title: Reports and letters
lessons.html:
Longer writing: plan, write, check

For a report or a letter, use three steps.

  1. Plan. Write down the main points you want to say, in order.
  2. Write. Turn the points into sentences. Use a new paragraph for each new idea.
  3. Check. Read it again. Fix spelling, missing words and wrong numbers. Ask: will the reader understand?

An incident report

If there is an accident or a near-miss, your supervisor may ask you to write what happened. Write only the facts:

  • date, time and place;
  • who was involved;
  • what happened, step by step;
  • what was done afterwards (first aid, machine switched off);
  • your name and signature.

On 3 June at about 08:15 in the feed store, Joseph Mokoena slipped on spilled maize and hurt his left wrist. I helped him up and called the first aider, Mrs Nkosi. She put on a sling and the manager drove him to the clinic.

A formal letter

A formal letter has a fixed layout:

  • your address and the date at the top;
  • the reader's name and address;
  • a greeting: "Dear Mr Botha" or "Dear Sir or Madam";
  • a subject line, for example "Application for tractor driver training";
  • the body: why you are writing, the details, and what you would like to happen;
  • an ending: "Yours faithfully" (if you do not know the name) or "Yours sincerely" (if you do), then your signature and name.

Keep a copy of important letters and forms you hand in.

Key points

  • Before writing, think about your purpose and your reader.
  • Messages should say who, what, when and where.
  • Read forms first and never sign what you do not understand.
  • Correct mistakes on records with one line and your initials.
  • For longer writing: plan, write, then check.
